newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unholy alliance in hostile French welcome to Pope.
newsitem.headline: Unholy alliance in hostile French welcome to Pope.

text.p: An unholy alliance will give Pope John Paul a rude welcome when he visits France from Thursday, including oddly-matched bedfellows such as communists, anarchists, Greens and freemasons.

So many causes have jumped on what the French press dubs the "Papophobia" bandwaggon -- a minority compared to the hundreds of thousands who will flock to his rallies -- that their message has become blurred.
But the hastily-erected rainbow coalition illustrates France's historical church-state divide, and a deep streak of anti-clericalism that has erupted repeatedly over the centuries.

No fewer than 65 different organisations are co-sponsoring an anti-pope march in Paris on Sunday, the day the Pontiff celebrates the 1,500th anniversary of the baptism of pagan king Clovis, the first European king to convert to Catholicism.
They include the anti-racist MRAP, the Young Socialists, the Greens, the National Union of Scientific Researchers, the Anarchist Federation, and the Communist Revolutionary League.

Some 50 celebrities have also backed the demonstration -- golden oldies crooner Jean Ferrat, film director Coline Serreau, cartoonist Sine, philosopher Daniel Bensaid and genetics professor Albert Jacquard.
Their joint statement appeals to "all republicans and democrats" to "defend the secular state (and) fight against the new moral order" which they say the Pontiff preaches.
Ask individual groups why they will be demonstrating, however, and the rally loses its focus.

Some organisations say they are demonstrating not so much against the Pope as against the Clovis celebration, or the presence of far-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, or public financing of the visit -- a cause espoused by the freemasons' Grand Orient lodge.
Others target papal teachings on abortion and contraception.

"Agreed, the message is getting blurred. But there is something extremely ambiguous about the context of the Pope's visit," said Mouloud Aounit, secretary-general of one of the leading associations, the Movement Against Racism and for Friendship Between Peoples (MRAP).

"We're not here to do anything anti-clerical or to fight the Pope. We want to say that the birth and identity of France are first and foremost about the values of the republic -- liberty, equality and fraternity," he said.

Several leftist groups bristled after Le Pen, whose anti-immigrant movement has hijacked Clovis as a symbol along with Joan of Arc, said he would attend Sunday's papal mass. The Church has said Le Pen is not invited and will not be admitted to the VIP enclosure in Reims.

Anti-papal activists accuse the French government of pandering to the National Front and to traditionalist Catholics by lionising Clovis, whom they portray as a Dark Ages warlord who converted out of political convenience, not faith.

"The whole masquerade around Clovis's baptism is a manipulation of the Catholic hierarchy by the extreme right," said Thierry Meyssan of the Reseau Voltaire, an umbrella group against the Pope's trip.

"There is no divide in France between Catholics and non-Catholics. There is a split between people who want a secular society and a very small part of the Church which is tied to the extreme-right," Meyssan said.
One newspaper even raised the prospect of a false pope showing up for a protest in Reims.

None of the numerous opposition movements has owned up to hiring a papal double but Le Figaro said anti-clerical militants planned to use him, at a cost of 7,000 francs ($1,400), during the Pontiff's rally.
